display_name: Plantagenet Omrah Pinot Noir, Great Southern
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Plantagenet Omrah Pinot Noir 2011 tastes like someone captured the cool edge of Great Southern in a bottle—red cherry, forest floor, and a granite snap you can trace straight back to the gravelly lateritic soils at the foot of the Porongurup Range. It’s a quiet $25-30 sleeper that drinks like a $50 Burgundy village wine, which explains why it disappears first whenever a mixed case lands in Perth or Sydney.",
  "wine_summary": "Plantagenet, founded in 1968, is the oldest winery in Great Southern and still bottles from those original, own-rooted vines; Omrah is their early-drinking Pinot label, built from parcels across Mount Barker and the Porongurup sub-regions. The 2011 vintage was cool and drawn-out—mean January temperature 2 °C below the 30-year norm—so ripeness parked at a modest 13% alc while skin phenolics hit full maturity, giving colour without weight and perfume without confected sweetness. That tension between cool climate acidity and granite-driven minerality is why Omrah punches above its price bracket; you’re tasting the region’s first serious attempt at Pinot, refreshed by a vintage that refused to get hot.",
  "terroir_expression": "Great Southern’s lateritic gravelly sandy loams—weathered ironstone over 1.4-billion-year-old gneiss and granite—drain fast yet hold just enough water for a slow, even ripening; that translates to bright red fruit with a wet-stone, ferrous edge you can literally smell after rain. Cold Southern-Ocean influence (Albany 30 km away) funnels afternoon breeze through the valleys, locking acidity at 7–8 g/L and shrinking berry size; the result is skin-to-juice ratio that gifts savoury, briary tannin without needing heavy extraction.",
  "vinification_summary": "Ferments are initiated wild in 2-ton open pots, 20% whole bunches layered in the middle to give carbonic spice while avoiding stalky greenness; daily hand-plunging lasts only eight days before pressing to limit tannin bleed. Maturation is split: seven months in older French barriques (minimum third-fill) for subtle oxygen, then a short spell in stainless to snap the fruit back into focus—this is why Omrah keeps its vibrant cranberry edge while the winery’s more serious ‘Mount Barker’ Pinot sees 40% new oak.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Nashville hot-fried chicken on white bread: the wine’s acidity and light tannins scrub cayenne oil and keep the palate awake.",
    "Mushroom and truffle risotto with a spoon of mascarpone: Porongurup granite minerality mirrors earthy porcini while bright cherry fruit lifts the dish.",
    "Rare-roasted salmon with beetroot and horseradish cream: cool-climate cranberry snap cuts the horseradish heat without overpowering delicate fish.",
    "Chinese five-spice roast duck pancakes: low alcohol and whole-bunch clove notes echo the spice mix, sandy tannin handles duck fat.",
    "Fine-dining: herb-crusted lamb loin, pink, with black-garlic jus—savoury stalk tannin and ironstone grit stand up to protein while acid slices the fat."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Kooyong Estate Pinot Noir — same granite base on Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula, similar cool-vintage snap but $10 dearer.",
    "Felton-Rockburn Pinot Noir — Central Otago, slightly darker fruit, same early-drinking intent and price bracket.",
    "Joseph Drouhin Bourgogge Pinot Noir — Burgundy’s limestone gives more chalk than granite, yet comparable weight, acidity, and week-night price."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Light-to-medium-bodied dry red with fine sandy tannin and ironstone minerality",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink now through 2026; cork shows no premature oxidation in 2011s but storage below 15 °C keeps the cranberry pop vivid.",
  "value_assessment": "A$24–30 on the shelf, and at that money it outruns Yarra Valley Pinot in the same bracket like Yering Station ($32) while giving 80% of the detail you’d pay $55 for in a Brokenwood Hunter. Worth it if you like savoury, mineral Pinot without oak makeup.",
  "market_position": "Restaurant by-the-glass lists in Perth and Melbourne feature it for margin (good cost, crowd-pleasing fruit) while independent retailers push it to Burgundy-curious shoppers who won’t stretch to $50; almost zero collector interest—people actually drink what they buy.",
  "insider_take": "Skip this if you chase plush, sweet Pinot; Omrah 11 is a bony, ferrous style that shows its granite roots more than primary fruit today. The bronze medal actually helps—keeps price sane while the wine quietly over-delivers for anyone who enjoys Chinon-like savouriness in red Burgundy clothing.",
  "aging_potential_years": 8,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 5,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 15,
  "sensory": {
    "acidity": 4,
    "tannin": 2,
    "body": 3,
    "sweetness": 1,
    "alcohol": 2,
    "color_intensity": "medium",
    "aroma_intensity": "medium",
    "finish_length": "medium",
    "complexity": "moderate",
    "quality_level": "good"
  }
}
